summary: Specifies an EDNS option so secondary DNS servers can honor the SOA EXPIRE field as if transferring from the primary, even through other secondaries. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Stored copies of a list should expire at a set time. This keeps the expiry time right even when copies are made from copies.

questions: how does dns zone expiry work
subtitle: Track how long DNS secondaries have been out of touch with the primary.

tldr.problem: DNS secondary servers are supposed to discard zone data after a timeout called SOA EXPIRE, but this does not work correctly when secondaries transfer from other secondaries rather than the primary.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7314 adds an EDNS option that carries the original SOA EXPIRE time through secondary-to-secondary transfers, so every secondary knows the real deadline regardless of transfer chain depth.
tldr.outcome: The secondary can stop serving stale zone data at the right time, even if it has been out of contact with the primary for a long time.

today: RFC 7314 is an Experimental RFC that allows DNS implementations to properly honor the SOA EXPIRE field when zones are transferred through chains of secondaries. It is not part of the Internet Standard.

sections.title: The Zone Expiry Problem
sections.content: In DNS, a primary server publishes a zone with an SOA EXPIRE field telling secondaries how long they may serve the zone if they lose contact with the primary. In a simple setup, secondaries refresh directly from the primary and the timeout works correctly. However, secondaries often transfer from other secondaries for robustness: secondary A copies from primary P, then secondary B copies from A. The problem: when B copies from A, there is no signal that both A and B should use the same expiry deadline based on the original primary's timing.
sections.plainLanguage: A photocopy of a list expires at a set date. If you make a copy of the copy, the new copy should expire on the same date, not later.

sections.title: The EDNS EXPIRE Option
sections.content: RFC 7314 solves this with a new EDNS option (code 9) that carries the remaining time before expiry. When a secondary makes a zone transfer request or refresh query to any server (primary or another secondary), it adds the zero-length option. The server responds with a 4-byte value showing either the original SOA EXPIRE (if it is the primary) or its current local expiry timer (if it is a secondary). The secondary then updates its own timer to the maximum of the value received and its current timer, never extending it, and following the rule that the SOA EXPIRE value itself acts as a cap.
sections.plainLanguage: When copying, ask "when does this expire?" and update your own expiry time to match the original, whichever is sooner.

sections.title: Secondary Behavior and Stale Data
sections.content: When a secondary receives an EDNS EXPIRE option in a response to an SOA query or a non-updating IXFR query (where the serial already matches), it updates its timer. After a zone transfer (AXFR or IXFR), the secondary prefers the EDNS EXPIRE value from the response over the SOA EXPIRE field in the zone itself, ensuring the expiry time is always the furthest original deadline. This mechanism prevents stale zone data from being served indefinitely when the secondary chain is broken from the primary.
sections.plainLanguage: A secondary stops serving the zone when the expiry time runs out, even if it has not heard from the primary in a long time.
